drills.title: vs Monsarichard (795) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Both your a2 and e2 pawns are one square from queening, and White's only hope is rushing the knight from b3 to c5 and then d3, where it blockades e2. Rf3 didn't cash in either pawn, so White got exactly that maneuver — Nc5, and after your check on d8 the knight landed on d3, turning a totally crushing position into merely a big one, a 6-pawn swing. The simple a1=R promotes immediately instead; even after Nxa1 you still have Rd8+ and Rd1+ hunting the king with an extra rook. When a pawn can queen right now, take it before looking for anything fancier.

drills.coachNote: With your rook on g4 and knight on c3 flooding in, White's only hope is getting the king to the e-file to babysit e2. Re4 let it just walk there — Kg3 next, and by the time you played the slow Kh7 the king had tucked in near the pawn, costing you nearly 4 pawns of advantage. Rf4+ was the move: it shoves the king to e3, away from easy defense, and after Rf1 you're already infiltrating the first rank, with Re8+ next keeping the king on the run. When you're pushing a pawn home, checks that drive the king backward beat quiet developing moves.

Before reaching for another idea, make sure the piece you've already committed isn't hanging.

Qb5 was the calm answer: it leaves g7 and h6 untouched to keep guarding your king while putting the queen to work, so the king shuffle that follows happens entirely on your terms.
